subject: e-washington-oath
text: George Washington took the first presidential oath of office on April 30, 1789, at Federal Hall in New York City.

sources.note: Gives Thursday, April 30 and Federal Hall, and says Chancellor Robert Livingston administered the oath.
States that Washington took the oath on April 30, 1789, in New York City, at Federal Hall.
Lists the first inauguration on April 30, 1789, in New York, with the oath taken outdoors; does not name Federal Hall.

subject: e-farewell
text: Washington's Farewell Address was first published in a Philadelphia newspaper, the American Daily Advertiser, on September 19, 1796.

sources.note: Says it was originally published in David C. Claypoole's American Daily Advertiser on September 19, 1796.
Says a Philadelphia newspaper published the address on September 19, 1796, in Claypoole's American Daily Advertiser.
Dates the address September 19, 1796 and says Washington released it to newspapers and never presented it in person; does not name the paper.

subject: e-jefferson-oath
text: Thomas Jefferson took the presidential oath on March 4, 1801, in the Senate chamber of the Capitol, at the first inauguration held in Washington, D.C.

sources.note: Gives March 4, 1801 and the Senate chamber of the Capitol for Jefferson's oath; does not itself call it the first in Washington.
Lists Jefferson's first inauguration on March 4, 1801 and calls it the first inauguration in Washington, D.C.
Gives March 4, 1801 and calls it the first inauguration held in Washington, D.C.; does not name the Senate chamber.

subject: e-louisiana
text: The treaty by which the United States bought the Louisiana Territory from France for $15 million was done at Paris and is dated April 30, 1803, during Thomas Jefferson's presidency.

sources.note: States the treaty was signed on April 30, 1803, that the price was $15 million, and that Jefferson approved the deal.
Reproduces the treaty's closing line: done at Paris on the 30th of April 1803.
Dates the Louisiana Purchase treaty to April 30, 1803 and gives the price as about $15 million; does not name Paris.

subject: e-capitol-burned
text: On August 24, 1814, during the War of 1812 and while James Madison was president, British forces burned the White House and the Capitol in Washington, D.C.

sources.note: States that on August 24, 1814, British forces marched into Washington and set fire to the White House, the Capitol and other buildings.
Dates the British burning of Washington to August 24, 1814 and says Madison and his government had left the capital.
States that on August 24, 1814, during the War of 1812, British troops burned the Capitol and almost all other public buildings; does not name Madison.

subject: e-removal-act
text: President Andrew Jackson signed the Indian Removal Act into law on May 28, 1830; it let the president negotiate exchanges of land west of the Mississippi River for tribal land inside existing states.

sources.note: Says President Jackson signed the bill into law on May 28, after the House passed it on May 26, 1830.
Gives the signing date as May 28, 1830 and says the act authorized the president to negotiate land exchanges west of the Mississippi.
Dates the signing to May 28, 1830 and says the act gave the president added powers to speed the removal of American Indian communities from the east; does not describe the land exchanges.

subject: e-fort-sumter
text: Confederate artillery opened fire on the Union-held Fort Sumter, in Charleston harbor, on April 12, 1861, the start of the Civil War.

sources.note: Dates the Confederate firing on Union-held Fort Sumter to April 12, 1861 and calls it the start of hostilities in the Civil War.
Says Confederate batteries opened fire on the fort on April 12 and that Major Anderson surrendered on April 13.
Says the bombardment began at 4:30 a.m. on April 12, 1861 and lasted about 34 hours.

subject: e-emancipation
text: Abraham Lincoln signed the final Emancipation Proclamation at the White House on January 1, 1863, declaring enslaved people in areas in rebellion against the United States to be free.

sources.note: Names Lincoln as the issuer and January 1, 1863 as the date, and quotes the declaration of freedom for people held as slaves in rebel states; does not name the White House.
States that Lincoln issued the proclamation on January 1, 1863 and quotes its freedom clause; does not name the White House.
Says Lincoln signed the final version on January 1, 1863, after greeting New Year's visitors at the White House.

subject: e-gettysburg
text: Abraham Lincoln delivered the Gettysburg Address on November 19, 1863, at the dedication of a cemetery for Union soldiers at Gettysburg, Pennsylvania.

sources.note: Dates the address November 19, 1863 and says Lincoln was invited to give remarks at the dedication of a cemetery for Union soldiers.
Says Lincoln delivered the speech on November 19, 1863, at the dedication of a national cemetery near the battlefield.
Dates the Gettysburg Address November 19, 1863 and says Lincoln gave it at the dedication of a national cemetery.

subject: e-lincoln-death
text: Abraham Lincoln was shot at Ford's Theatre on the night of April 14, 1865, and died the next morning, April 15, 1865.

sources.note: Says Booth shot Lincoln at Ford's Theatre on April 14, 1865 and that Lincoln died at 7:22 am on April 15.
Says Lincoln was shot at Ford's Theater on April 14 and died at 7:22 a.m. the next morning.
Says Lincoln was shot at Ford's Theatre on April 14, 1865 and died the next morning.

subject: e-roosevelt-sworn
text: William McKinley, shot on September 6, 1901, died on September 14, 1901, and Theodore Roosevelt took the presidential oath the same day in Buffalo, New York.

sources.note: Says McKinley died on September 14, 1901 and Roosevelt took the oath that afternoon in Buffalo.
Says McKinley was shot on September 6, 1901 at the Pan-American Exposition in Buffalo, died on September 14, and Roosevelt became president.
Says Roosevelt took the oath on September 14, 1901 in Buffalo after McKinley died, and that McKinley was shot on September 6.

subject: e-22nd-amendment
text: The 22nd Amendment, which says no person may be elected president more than twice, was ratified on February 27, 1951, after Franklin Roosevelt had won four elections.

sources.note: Gives 'Ratified February 27, 1951' and quotes the two-election limit; does not mention Roosevelt.
Marks February 27 as the ratification anniversary and says the amendment was introduced two years after Roosevelt's fourth inauguration.
Says Minnesota's approval on February 27, 1951 completed ratification and ties the amendment to Roosevelt's four consecutive terms.

subject: e-kennedy
text: President John F. Kennedy was shot while riding in a motorcade in Dallas, Texas, on November 22, 1963, and died that day.

sources.note: Says Kennedy was shot in Dallas at about 12:30 p.m. on November 22, 1963 and that Lyndon Johnson was then sworn in as president.
Dates the Dallas motorcade shooting to November 22, 1963 and says Kennedy died soon after at Parkland Memorial Hospital.
Says Johnson took the oath on November 22, 1963, about two hours after Kennedy's assassination, which shows Kennedy died that day.

subject: e-nixon-resigns
text: Richard Nixon announced on August 8, 1974 that he would resign, and his resignation took effect at noon on August 9, 1974, making him the first U.S. president to resign.

sources.note: Says Nixon announced on August 8, 1974 that he would resign effective at noon the next day, and calls him the first sitting president to resign.
Says Nixon became the first and only president to resign, effective August 9, 1974, quoting 'effective at noon tomorrow'.
Says Gerald Ford took the oath of office on August 9, 1974, on Nixon's resignation.

subject: c-bastille
text: On July 14, 1789, Parisians stormed the Bastille fortress in Paris, an event commonly linked with the start of the French Revolution.

sources.note: Says Jefferson witnessed events in Paris on July 14, 1789 that are commonly seen as the start of the French Revolution.
Says the Bastille fortress was stormed on July 14, 1789 by Parisian revolutionaries.
Says thousands of Parisians stormed the prison on July 14, 1789.

subject: c-waterloo
text: On June 18, 1815, Napoleon's French army fought an allied army under the Duke of Wellington, joined by Marshal Blucher's forces, at the Battle of Waterloo.

sources.note: Says the battle was fought on 18 June 1815 between Napoleon's army and a coalition led by Wellington and Blucher.
Describes the fighting on Sunday 18th June.
Says the battle began on Sunday, June 18, 1815.

subject: c-origin
text: Charles Darwin's book On the Origin of Species was published on November 24, 1859.

sources.note: States that the book was published on 24 November 1859.
Lists 24 November 1859 as the day On the Origin of Species was published.
Says the Origin was published on 24 November 1859, in a first printing of 1,250 copies.

subject: c-sarajevo
text: Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria and his wife Sophie were shot in Sarajevo on June 28, 1914, and both died.

sources.note: Lists June 28, 1914 as the day the archduke and his wife were killed by an assassin's bullets in Sarajevo.
Says Gavrilo Princip shot both the archduke and his wife in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914.
Describes Sunday morning, June 28, 1914 in Sarajevo, when the archduke and his wife were fatally shot.

subject: c-sputnik
text: The Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first artificial Earth satellite, on October 4, 1957.

sources.note: Says the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1 on October 4, 1957.
Says the Soviet Union launched the first artificial satellite, Sputnik-1, on October 4, 1957.
Says the Soviet Union launched the world's first artificial satellite on October 4, 1957.

subject: c-apollo
text: The lunar module of Apollo 11 landed on the Moon at Tranquility Base on July 20, 1969.

sources.note: Says the lunar module landed on July 20, 1969 and quotes Armstrong's call from Tranquility Base.
Gives the landing time as 20:17:40 GMT on July 20, 1969; does not name Tranquility Base.
Heads its mission overview with the landing on July 20 and the call from Tranquility Base.

subject: c-berlin-wall
text: On the night of November 9, 1989, an East German announcement about travel changes brought crowds to the Berlin Wall, and the border crossings were opened.

sources.note: Says the wall came down on the evening of November 9, 1989, after an East German press-conference announcement of travel changes.
Says that on November 9, 1989 thousands of Germans brought down the Berlin Wall.
Says that on the night of November 9, 1989 an East German announcement led crowds to the checkpoints, where guards opened the gates.

subject: e-gettysburg
value: written on the back of an envelope on the train to Gettysburg
text: The popular story that Lincoln wrote the Gettysburg Address on the back of an envelope during the train ride to Gettysburg is not supported by the sources.
alternatives: Lincoln drafted the first part in Washington on Executive Mansion stationery and finished revising it at the David Wills house in Gettysburg.

sources.note: Calls the envelope story perhaps the biggest myth about the address, and says the surviving drafts are in steady handwriting, not the handwriting of a moving train.
Says the first page of the earliest known draft, the Nicolay copy, is on Executive Mansion stationery, which suggests it was drafted in Washington.
Says Lincoln made his final revisions in a bedroom at the Wills house in Gettysburg; it does not mention an envelope.

subject: e-gettysburg
value: at the David Wills house in Gettysburg, evening of November 18 or November 19, 1863
text: Lincoln finished revising the Gettysburg Address at the David Wills house in Gettysburg, but the sources differ on whether the last rewrite came on the evening of November 18 or on November 19, 1863.
alternatives: The evening of November 18, 1863, after he arrived in Gettysburg (National Park Service).
November 19, 1863, the day of the ceremony, for the final paragraph of the Nicolay copy (Library of Congress).

sources.note: Says Lincoln stayed at the Wills house on November 18 and made his final revisions in the bedroom before delivering the address the next day.
Says the second page of the Nicolay copy is on different paper, suggesting Lincoln rewrote the final paragraph in Gettysburg on November 19.
Says Lincoln finalized the speech after arriving in Gettysburg; it does not give the hour.

subject: e-emancipation
value: freed every enslaved person in the United States
text: The common belief that the Emancipation Proclamation freed every enslaved person in the United States on January 1, 1863 is not supported by the sources: it named areas in rebellion and left out the border states.
alternatives: It declared people held as slaves in areas in rebellion to be free and left out the border states of Maryland, Kentucky and Missouri (National Park Service).
It did not end slavery everywhere, though it changed the character of the war (Library of Congress).

sources.note: Quotes the proclamation's own wording about areas in rebellion and says the freedom it promised depended on Union military victory.
Says the final proclamation named areas in rebellion and notably left out the border states of Maryland, Kentucky and Missouri.
Says the proclamation did not end slavery, and quotes its wording that covers people held as slaves in states, or parts of states, in rebellion.

subject: e-washington-oath
value: Washington added the words so help me God
short: Washington's first oath: the added words
text: The popular story that Washington added the words "so help me God" to his first presidential oath is not supported by the sources: no account written at the time records it, and it first appears in print in 1854.
alternatives: The oath written in the Constitution does not contain those words, and the first confirmed use of them by a president was Chester Arthur's in 1881 (History News Network).

sources.note: Says Washington Irving claimed Washington began the practice and that there is no direct evidence of it.
A history professor emeritus argues there is no contemporary evidence that Washington changed the oath, and that the account of the French minister who attended records the oath without those words.
A history professor says the story first appeared in print in 1854 and that no contemporary evidence for it survives.

subject: e-emancipation
text: The Civil War that began with the firing on Fort Sumter in April 1861 is one of the causes of the Emancipation Proclamation, which Lincoln issued in January 1863 as a war measure; the sources also point to the Union victory at Antietam in 1862 as a cause.

sources.note: Says the proclamation was issued as a war measure for suppressing the rebellion, a few days after the Union victory at Antietam.
Calls the proclamation a decisive war measure that deprived the South of enslaved labor for its war effort.
Says Lincoln called for volunteers after the attack on Fort Sumter, then announced emancipation as a war strategy once the Antietam victory gave him the military success he wanted.

subject: e-22nd-amendment
text: Washington's announcement in his Farewell Address that he would not seek a third term is one of the causes of the 22nd Amendment: the sources trace a two-term custom to his example, and name Franklin Roosevelt's four election wins as what led Congress to write the custom into law.
alternatives: Washington's decision not to seek a third term set the unwritten two-term custom that the 22nd Amendment later made law (National Constitution Center, Annenberg Classroom).
Some scholars credit Thomas Jefferson more than Washington with making the two-term custom a norm (PBS NewsHour).

sources.note: Says Washington set an unofficial precedent in 1796 by deciding not to seek a third term, and that Roosevelt's four wins led Congress to propose the amendment.
Says commentators often cite Washington's choice as the start of the two-term custom, though some scholars credit Jefferson more, and that Roosevelt's third and fourth terms led to the amendment.
Says Washington set a precedent by declining a third term, that it lasted until 1940, and that Congress proposed the amendment after Roosevelt's death in 1945.

subject: c-apollo
text: The launch of Sputnik 1 in 1957 is one of the causes of the Moon landing: it began the space race and led to the creation of NASA, and President Kennedy set the goal of landing on the Moon in 1961 within that race. No single source states the whole chain, so each source below confirms one step.

sources.note: Says the launch of Sputnik fueled the space race and led U.S. policymakers to speed up space programs (step one).
Says the Sputnik launch led directly to the creation of NASA in 1958 (step two).
Reprints Kennedy's 1961 Moon goal and links the pressure on him to the Sputnik shock and Gagarin's flight (step three).
Describes the U.S.-Soviet rivalry from Sputnik, through NASA's creation and Kennedy's Moon goal, to Apollo 11 winning the Moon race in July 1969 (step four).

subject: e-gettysburg
text: Edward Everett gave the main oration at the cemetery dedication on November 19, 1863 and spoke for about two hours; Lincoln spoke after him for about two minutes.

sources.note: Says Everett gave a two-hour oration and that Lincoln's remarks lasted roughly two minutes.
Says Lincoln was not the main speaker, that Everett gave a long oration, and that Lincoln spoke for roughly two minutes.
Says Everett spoke for two hours before Lincoln, and describes Everett's letter that compares his two hours with Lincoln's two minutes.
Describes Everett's letter of November 20, 1863, written as the main speaker, setting his two hours beside Lincoln's two minutes.

subject: e-gettysburg
text: Lincoln arrived in Gettysburg on the evening of November 18, 1863 and stayed at the house of David Wills.

sources.note: Says Lincoln arrived on the evening of November 18, 1863 and stayed at the Wills home.
Says Lincoln came to Gettysburg on the evening of November 18, was escorted to the Wills home, and describes the visit as an overnight stay.
Places Lincoln at Judge Wills's home in Gettysburg when he revised the final paragraph; does not give his hour of arrival.

subject: e-gettysburg
text: The address describes the Civil War as a test of whether a nation founded on liberty and equality can last, and calls on the living to carry on the unfinished work of the soldiers who died there.

sources.note: Gives the full text, which frames the war as a test of such a nation and calls on the living to finish the unfinished work.
Gives the full text and the same summary of its argument.
Says Lincoln argued that the war tested whether a nation founded on liberty and equality could endure.

subject: e-gettysburg
text: Five handwritten copies of the Gettysburg Address by Lincoln are known.

sources.note: Says five known manuscript copies exist and that the Library of Congress holds two of them.
Says five copies are known and names who each was written for.
Says Lincoln wrote five manuscript versions, and describes where each is held.

subject: e-emancipation
text: The final Emancipation Proclamation, taking effect on January 1, 1863, declared free the people held as slaves in states or parts of states that were then in rebellion against the United States.

sources.note: Quotes the freedom clause that covers people held as slaves in states, or parts of states, in rebellion.
Says the proclamation declared free those held as slaves in the rebel states it names.
Says the final version freed enslaved people in areas in rebellion, covering most of the South.

subject: e-emancipation
text: The proclamation did not cover slave states that stayed in the Union, such as Maryland, Kentucky and Missouri, or parts of the Confederacy already under Union control.

sources.note: Says it excluded the border states of Maryland, Kentucky and Missouri and left areas under United States control unaffected.
Says it exempted parts of the Confederacy under Union control and left slavery in place in the loyal border states.
Says the final proclamation freed slaves in Confederate or contested areas and left out the border states and Union-controlled Confederate territory.

subject: e-emancipation
text: The proclamation opened the armed forces of the United States to freed Black men.

sources.note: Gives the text, which says freed men of suitable condition will be received into the armed service.
Says it allowed nearly 180,000 former slaves and free Black men to serve as United States Colored Troops.
Says the proclamation authorized the recruitment of African Americans as Union soldiers.

subject: e-emancipation
text: Lincoln issued a preliminary proclamation on September 22, 1862, after the Union victory at Antietam, warning that the final order would follow on January 1, 1863 if the rebellion continued.

sources.note: Gives September 22, 1862, after the Battle of Antietam, for the preliminary proclamation.
Says Lincoln issued the preliminary proclamation on September 22, 1862 and links it to the Antietam victory.
Dates the preliminary proclamation to September 22, 1862, after Antietam, and says it warned of the January 1 order.

subject: e-emancipation
text: Lincoln issued the proclamation in his role as commander in chief and described it as a war measure to put down the rebellion.

sources.note: Gives the text, in which Lincoln invokes his power as commander in chief and calls the order a fit and necessary war measure.
Says Lincoln grounded the order in his authority as commander in chief during the rebellion.
Says the order was issued under his powers as commander in chief and describes it as a war measure.

subject: e-emancipation
text: Slavery was ended throughout the United States by the Thirteenth Amendment, ratified on December 6, 1865.

sources.note: Gives December 6, 1865 for ratification and says the amendment abolished slavery throughout the United States.

subject: e-fort-sumter
text: In early March 1861 Major Robert Anderson, who commanded Fort Sumter in Charleston harbor, reported that his garrison needed fresh supplies. President Abraham Lincoln could withdraw the garrison, try to reinforce the fort with troops, or send supplies only.

sources.note: Describes the garrison's shortage and names three courses: evacuation, supply and reinforcement.
In Lincoln's own account to Congress, weighs giving up the fort, reinforcing it and sending provisions.
Says Anderson told the new president the fort needed resupply or evacuation.

subject: e-fort-sumter
text: Lincoln chose to send provisions only. He told the governor of South Carolina that no men, arms or ammunition would be landed unless the supply attempt was resisted.

sources.note: Says Lincoln ordered a supply attempt with provisions only and no men, arms or ammunition unless the expedition was attacked.
Lincoln says he prepared an expedition to provision, not reinforce, the fort and told South Carolina's governor so.
Says Lincoln chose to send provisions but no additional troops or ordnance unless resistance was met.

subject: e-fort-sumter
text: Confederate guns opened fire on Fort Sumter at 4:30 a.m. on April 12, 1861, and Major Anderson surrendered the fort on April 13.

subject: e-louisiana
text: In 1803 Thomas Jefferson doubted that the Constitution gave the federal government the power to buy new territory. He considered asking for a constitutional amendment first.

subject: e-louisiana
text: Jefferson dropped the amendment idea, partly because Napoleon had threatened to withdraw from the deal, and submitted the treaty to the Senate on October 17, 1803.

text: The Senate ratified the Louisiana Purchase treaty on October 20, 1803, by a vote of 24 to 7.

subject: e-farewell
text: Before the election of 1792 George Washington had thought about leaving office after his first term, and a farewell address was prepared for that purpose. He could retire then or serve a second term.

text: Washington decided to serve a second term and was inaugurated for it on March 4, 1793.

text: Four years later, in the Farewell Address published on September 19, 1796, Washington announced that he would not seek a third term.
